prompt: What is the botanical name of the oil palm?

options.text: Elaeis guineensis
Cocos nucifera
Manihot esculenta
Oryza sativa

explanation: Elaeis guineensis. It is the only botanical name in the whole course, which makes it a certainty for a names question.

why.a: Correct. Elaeis guineensis is the oil palm.
why.b: Wrong. Cocos nucifera is the coconut palm.
why.c: Wrong. Manihot esculenta is cassava, which appears here only as an intercrop.
why.d: Wrong. Oryza sativa is rice, which appears in rice-fish culture.

prompt: The botanical name of the oil palm is Elaeis {{1}}.
explanation: Guineensis. The name points at its West African origin, which is also the first region the text names for its cultivation.

prompt: Elaeis guineensis is the primary source of which three products?

options.text: Palm oil, palm kernel oil, and palm kernel meal
Palm wine, raffia and thatch
Coconut oil, copra and coir
Groundnut oil, cake and shell

explanation: Palm oil, palm kernel oil, palm kernel meal. These serve as raw materials for edible vegetable oils, soaps, cosmetics and animal feed.

why.a: Correct. These three are the products the introduction names.
why.b: Wrong. None of these appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Those are coconut products.
why.d: Wrong. Those are groundnut products.

prompt: Oil palm products are important raw materials for edible vegetable oils, soaps, cosmetics and animal {{1}}.
explanation: Animal feed. Palm kernel cake is the by-product that supplies it, which is why feed appears this early in the unit.

prompt: Oil palm products are used only as edible vegetable oils and have no industrial application.
explanation: The introduction names soaps, cosmetics and animal feed alongside edible oils, and later the unit adds biodiesel, biomass energy, animal bedding and biodegradable building materials.

why.true: Wrong. Only is an absolute, and the text lists several non-food uses.
why.false: Correct. Soaps, cosmetics, animal feed and biofuel are all named.

prompt: Which part of the oil palm fruit gives palm oil, and which gives palm kernel oil?

options.text: Palm oil comes from the mesocarp, the fleshy outer part; palm kernel oil comes from the kernel
Palm oil comes from the kernel; palm kernel oil comes from the mesocarp
Both come from the kernel
Both come from the shell

explanation: Mesocarp for palm oil, kernel for palm kernel oil. Getting this the wrong way round makes half of Module Three impossible.

why.a: Correct. Mesocarp gives palm oil; kernel gives palm kernel oil.
why.b: Wrong. This reverses the two.
why.c: Wrong. The mesocarp is the source of palm oil.
why.d: Wrong. The shell, the endocarp, yields no oil; it is what Dura has thickly and Pisifera barely at all.

prompt: Palm oil is produced from the {{1}}, the fleshy outer part of the fruit.
explanation: Mesocarp. The glossary calls it the fleshy middle layer of the fruit, from which palm oil is extracted.

prompt: In which three regions is oil palm widely grown?

options.text: West Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America
North Africa, Central Asia, and Northern Europe
The Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Australia
Only Nigeria

explanation: West Africa, Southeast Asia, South America. All three are tropical, which follows from the temperature and rainfall requirements.

why.a: Correct. These are the three regions named.
why.b: Wrong. None is tropical enough for a crop needing 25 to 34 degrees Celsius.
why.c: Wrong. None of these is named in the text.
why.d: Wrong, and an absolute. Nigeria is in West Africa, but it is not the only region.

prompt: Oil palm is a tropical {{1}} crop cultivated mainly for its fruits.
explanation: Perennial. It is why the first harvest comes 3 to 4 years after planting and why intercropping is limited to the first 4 years.

prompt: What kind of soil does oil palm require?

options.text: Deep, fertile, well-drained loamy soils
Shallow sandy soils with poor drainage
Waterlogged clay soils
Rocky upland soils

explanation: Deep, fertile, well-drained and loamy, in lowland regions with high rainfall and abundant sunlight.

why.a: Correct. All four adjectives come from the environmental requirements.
why.b: Wrong. Shallow and poorly drained is the opposite of what is required.
why.c: Wrong. Well-drained is specified, so waterlogging is ruled out.
why.d: Wrong. Lowland is specified, and terrain should be flat, rolling or gently sloping.

prompt: What is the optimal temperature range for oil palm cultivation?

options.text: 25 to 34 degrees Celsius
25 to 30 degrees Celsius
5 to 8 degrees Celsius
40 degrees Celsius

explanation: 25 to 34 degrees Celsius. The 25 to 30 answer is the tilapia range from Module Two and shares the lower bound, which is exactly the sort of near miss this course rewards you for spotting.

why.a: Correct. The optimal temperature for oil palm is 25 to 34 degrees Celsius.
why.b: Wrong. 25 to 30 degrees is where tilapia thrives, in the fish farming unit.
why.c: Wrong. 5 to 8 mg/L is the dissolved oxygen requirement, not a temperature.
why.d: Wrong. 40 degrees for 70 to 80 days is the dormancy-breaking treatment for seeds.

prompt: The optimal temperature for oil palm is 25 to {{1}} degrees Celsius.
explanation: 34. Hold the pair together: 25 to 34 for oil palm, 25 to 30 for tilapia.

prompt: What annual rainfall does oil palm require?
explanation: 2000 to 2500 mm annually. High rainfall is the first environmental condition the text names.

why.a: Correct. The stated requirement is 2000 to 2500 mm annually.
why.b: Wrong. That is semi-arid rainfall, far below the requirement.
why.c: Wrong. Below the stated range.
why.d: Wrong. Above the stated range.

prompt: Oil palm requires an annual rainfall of {{1}} mm.
explanation: 2000 to 2500 mm. Together with 25 to 34 degrees and pH 5.0 to 6.0, these are the three environmental figures.

prompt: What soil pH does oil palm require?

options.text: 5.0 to 6.0, that is slightly acidic
7.0 exactly, that is neutral
8.5 to 9.5, that is alkaline

explanation: 5.0 to 6.0, slightly acidic. The 6.5 to 8.5 answer is the water pH range for rearing fish, and mixing the two up is the classic Module Two and Module Three collision.

why.a: Correct. The glossary calls it slightly acidic, pH 5.0 to 6.0.
why.b: Wrong. 6.5 to 8.5 is the pH range for fish in water.
why.c: Wrong. Neutral is above the stated range.
why.d: Wrong. Alkaline soil is well outside the requirement.

prompt: The soil pH for oil palm is 5.0 to {{1}}.
explanation: 6.0. Say the units out loud: soil pH 5.0 to 6.0 for the palm, water pH 6.5 to 8.5 for the fish.

prompt: Oil palm cannot grow at all in seasonally wet or dry areas.
explanation: It can grow there, although yields may be lower under such conditions. The word cannot is what makes the statement false.

why.true: Wrong. The text allows growth in seasonally wet or dry areas, with reduced yield.
why.false: Correct. It grows, but yields may be lower.

prompt: Which set gives the five key stages of oil palm cultivation, in order?

options.text: Propagation, nursery management, field establishment, agronomic practices, harvesting
Sterilisation, threshing, digesting, pressing, clarification
Fibre separation, nut drying, cracking, extraction, storage
Planning, organising, directing, controlling, reviewing

explanation: Propagation through harvesting. The sterilisation and threshing answer is the fresh fruit bunch processing sequence, and the fibre separation and cracking answer is the palm kernel sequence, so all three fives in Module Three appear here together.

why.a: Correct. These are the five cultivation stages in order.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the five processing stages of fresh fruit bunches.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the five palm kernel processing stages.
why.d: Wrong. Those are close to POCD, the operations management framework in Module Four.

prompt: Oil palm cultivation has {{1}} key stages.
explanation: Five. Module Three has three separate lists of five: cultivation stages, fruit processing stages, and kernel processing stages.

prompt: How is oil palm commonly propagated, and what alternative does the text mention?

options.text: Commonly through seeds, with vegetative propagation through tissue culture used in research and specialised practice
Commonly by cuttings, with seeds used only in research
Only by tissue culture
By grafting onto coconut rootstock

explanation: Seeds first, tissue culture second. The glossary agrees: propagation is reproducing oil palm plants, commonly through seeds or tissue culture.

why.a: Correct. Seeds commonly, tissue culture in research and specialised practice.
why.b: Wrong. This reverses the two.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. Seeds are the common route.
why.d: Wrong. No grafting is described in the course.

prompt: Which cross produces the most commercially desirable oil palm variety?

options.text: Dura crossed with Pisifera, producing Tenera
Tenera crossed with Dura, producing Pisifera
Pisifera crossed with Tenera, producing Dura
Nigrescens crossed with Virescens, producing Albescens

explanation: Dura by Pisifera gives Tenera, and Tenera is preferred because of its higher oil yield. The Nigrescens and Virescens answer confuses the varieties with the fruit types, which are a different classification.

why.a: Correct. Dura and Pisifera are crossed to produce the hybrid Tenera.
why.b: Wrong. Tenera is the product of the cross, not a parent.
why.c: Wrong. Dura is a parent, not the offspring.
why.d: Wrong. Those are fruit types, which describe external morphology rather than genetics.

prompt: The Dura and Pisifera varieties are crossed to produce the hybrid {{1}}.
explanation: Tenera. It is the most commercially desirable type because of its higher oil yield.

prompt: How is seed dormancy broken in oil palm?

options.text: By treating the seeds at 40 degrees Celsius for approximately 70 to 80 days
By soaking the seeds in water for 12 to 15 months
By chilling the seeds at 5 degrees Celsius for 30 days
By boiling the seeds at 140 to 150 degrees Celsius for 60 to 90 minutes

explanation: 40 degrees Celsius for 70 to 80 days. The 140 to 150 degrees answer is the sterilisation treatment for fresh fruit bunches from the processing unit, and the 12 to 15 months answer borrows the nursery duration.

why.a: Correct. Dormancy is broken at 40 degrees Celsius for approximately 70 to 80 days.
why.b: Wrong. 12 to 15 months is how long seedlings stay in the nursery.
why.c: Wrong. No chilling treatment appears in the course.
why.d: Wrong. That is sterilisation of harvested fruit bunches, not seed treatment.

prompt: Oil palm seed dormancy is broken at 40 degrees Celsius for approximately {{1}} days.
explanation: 70 to 80 days. Beware 60 to 90, which is the sterilisation time in minutes, not days.

prompt: How long are oil palm seedlings raised in the nursery before transplanting to the field?

options.text: About 12 to 15 months
About 70 to 80 days
About 3 to 4 years
About 60 to 90 minutes

explanation: 12 to 15 months, in black polythene bags. Note that the self-assessment answer gives 12 to 18 months, which is a discrepancy inside the course text itself; the unit body says 12 to 15.

why.a: Correct. The unit gives 12 to 15 months in black polythene bags.
why.b: Wrong. 70 to 80 days is the dormancy-breaking treatment.
why.c: Wrong. 3 to 4 years is the time to first harvest after planting.
why.d: Wrong. 60 to 90 minutes is the sterilisation time.

prompt: Oil palm seedlings are raised in black polythene bags for about {{1}} months.
explanation: 12 to 15 months. The bags are black and perforated at the bottom so excess water can drain out.

prompt: Why are the nursery polythene bags perforated at the bottom?

options.text: To allow excess water to drain out
To let the roots grow into the ground
To let air reach the seed
To make the bags lighter to carry

explanation: Drainage. It fits the wider requirement for well-drained soils: oil palm needs high rainfall but not waterlogging.

why.a: Correct. The bags are perforated so excess water can drain out.
why.b: Wrong. Seedlings are transplanted, so roots are meant to stay in the bag.
why.c: Wrong. Aeration of the seed is not the stated reason.
why.d: Wrong. Weight is not mentioned.

prompt: Which three qualities should an ideal nursery site have?

options.text: Near a reliable source of water, easily accessible to workers and vehicles, and relatively close to the field
On a steep slope, far from roads, and shaded all year
Beside a market, near a river, and fenced with CCTV
On sandy soil, with no shade, and far from the planting site

explanation: Water, access, proximity. Each is practical: seedlings need watering, workers need to reach them, and the transplant journey should be short.

why.a: Correct. These three are the nursery site requirements.
why.b: Wrong. Terrain should be flat, rolling or gently sloping, and access matters.
why.c: Wrong. Fencing and CCTV are the fish farm security principle.
why.d: Wrong. Shading in the dry season is a nursery practice, and proximity is required.

prompt: Nursery establishment should begin during the early {{1}} season.
explanation: Early rainy season. Field planting is also at the beginning of the rainy season, so the whole calendar runs on the rains.

prompt: At what rate is fertiliser applied in the oil palm nursery?

options.text: 56 g per seedling bag
12 g per seedling bag
143 g per seedling bag
560 g per seedling bag

explanation: 56 grams per bag. It is a small, precise figure of exactly the kind a numbers question is built on.

why.a: Correct. The nursery rate is 56 g per seedling bag.
why.b: Wrong. 12 is the first two numbers of the NPKMg ratio 12:12:17:2.
why.c: Wrong. 143 is the number of palms per hectare.
why.d: Wrong. Ten times the stated rate.

prompt: Fertiliser is applied in the nursery at a rate of {{1}} g per seedling bag.
explanation: 56 g. Module Three's four numbers to hold apart are 56 g, 143 palms, 9 m by 9 m, and 12:12:17:2.

prompt: Which of these is one of the important nursery practices named in the text?

options.text: Shading during the dry season to reduce water stress
Pruning old and dead leaves
Pegging planting positions
Harvesting loose fruits

explanation: Shading in the dry season. Pruning is an agronomic practice, pegging is field establishment, and harvesting is the last stage entirely.

why.a: Correct. Shading during the dry season is a nursery practice.
why.b: Wrong. Pruning belongs to agronomic practices in the field.
why.c: Wrong. Pegging is part of land preparation for field establishment.
why.d: Wrong. Harvesting comes 3 to 4 years after field planting.

prompt: {{1}} conserves moisture and suppresses weeds in the nursery.
explanation: Mulching. The glossary adds a third benefit: it reduces erosion.

prompt: What three operations make up land preparation for oil palm?

options.text: Clearing vegetation, ploughing the land, and pegging planting positions
Weeding, fertilising and pruning
Mulching, shading and watering
Sterilising, threshing and digesting

explanation: Clear, plough, peg. The weeding and fertilising answer is agronomic practices, the mulching and shading answer is nursery care, and the sterilising and threshing answer is processing, so all three wrong answers are neighbouring lists.

why.a: Correct. These three are land preparation.
why.b: Wrong. Those are agronomic practices after establishment.
why.c: Wrong. Those are nursery practices.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the first three fruit processing stages.

prompt: Suitable land for oil palm has flat, rolling or gently {{1}} terrain.
explanation: Gently sloping. Steep land is ruled out, which fits the requirement for well-drained soil without erosion.

prompt: What is the recommended spacing for oil palm, and how many palms per hectare does it give?

options.text: 9 m by 9 m in a triangular pattern, giving approximately 143 palms per hectare
9 m by 9 m in a square pattern, giving approximately 123 palms per hectare
5 m by 5 m in a triangular pattern, giving approximately 400 palms per hectare
12 m by 12 m in a square pattern, giving approximately 69 palms per hectare

explanation: 9 m by 9 m triangular, about 143 palms per hectare. The triangular arrangement is why the figure is 143 rather than the 123 that square spacing at 9 m would give.

why.a: Correct. 9 m by 9 m triangular, approximately 143 palms per hectare.
why.b: Wrong. The pattern is triangular, not square, and the text gives 143.
why.c: Wrong. No 5 m spacing appears in the course.
why.d: Wrong. No 12 m spacing appears in the course.

prompt: Spacing of 9 m by 9 m in a triangular pattern gives approximately {{1}} palms per hectare.
explanation: 143. Watch the digits: 143, not 134. It is the most transposable number in the whole course.

prompt: What does triangular spacing mean, according to the glossary?

options.text: Each tree is planted at equal distance, forming an equilateral triangle
Trees are planted in rows of three
The plantation is laid out in a triangular field
Every third tree is removed after four years

explanation: Equal distances forming an equilateral triangle. That geometry is what packs 143 palms into a hectare at 9 m spacing.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary definition.
why.b: Wrong. Rows of three is not what the term means.
why.c: Wrong. The shape of the field is not the point.
why.d: Wrong. No thinning schedule appears in the course.

prompt: In triangular spacing each tree is planted at equal distance, forming an {{1}} triangle.
explanation: Equilateral. Equal sides, which is what equal spacing in every direction produces.

prompt: When is oil palm planted in the field, and why?

options.text: At the beginning of the rainy season, to ensure adequate soil moisture
At the height of the dry season, to reduce fungal disease
Immediately after harvest of the previous crop, whatever the season
In the middle of the rainy season, to avoid erosion

explanation: Beginning of the rains, for soil moisture. The nursery is established in the early rainy season too, so both moves follow the same signal.

why.a: Correct. Planting is at the beginning of the rainy season for adequate soil moisture.
why.b: Wrong. Dry season planting would leave the seedling without water.
why.c: Wrong. The timing is tied to the rains, not to a previous crop.
why.d: Wrong. The text says the beginning of the season, not the middle.

prompt: Planting is usually done at the beginning of the rainy season to ensure adequate soil {{1}}.
explanation: Moisture. It is the reason the calendar matters: a young palm planted into dry soil will not establish.

prompt: What are the four routine agronomic practices for oil palm?

options.text: Weeding, fertilizer application, pruning, and pest and disease control
Clearing, ploughing, pegging, and planting
Mulching, shading, watering, and hardening off
Sorting, grading, drying, and packing

explanation: Weeding, fertiliser, pruning, pest and disease control. The glossary gives the same four as its definition of agronomic practices.

why.a: Correct. These four are the routine agronomic practices.
why.b: Wrong. Those are land preparation and establishment.
why.c: Wrong. Those are nursery practices.
why.d: Wrong. Those are post-harvest and value addition operations.

prompt: There are {{1}} routine agronomic practices for oil palm: weeding, fertilizer application, pruning, and pest and disease control.
explanation: Four. Note how neatly Module Three counts: 5 cultivation stages, 4 agronomic practices, 6 pests and diseases, 5 fruit types, 3 varieties.

prompt: Which fertilizer is commonly recommended for oil palm?

options.text: Urea at 56 g per palm

explanation: NPKMg in the ratio 12:12:17:2. Note that potassium, the 17, is the largest share, which is characteristic of oil palm nutrition.

why.a: Correct. The recommended fertilizer is NPKMg 12:12:17:2.
why.b: Wrong. No such ratio appears in the course, and it omits magnesium.
why.c: Wrong. The figures are transposed; 17 belongs in the third position.
why.d: Wrong. 56 g is the nursery application rate, not a field fertilizer type.

prompt: The commonly recommended fertilizer for oil palm is NPKMg in the ratio {{1}}.
explanation: 12:12:17:2. Four numbers for four nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium.

prompt: Pruning removes old or dead leaves to achieve which three things?

options.text: Improve air circulation, reduce pest habitats, and facilitate harvesting
Increase fruit size, deepen colour, and raise oil content
Reduce water use, lower the canopy, and slow growth
Prevent flowering, delay fruiting, and extend the nursery period

explanation: Air circulation, pest habitat, harvesting access. The glossary adds that pruning removes fronds to encourage healthy growth and easier harvesting.

why.a: Correct. These three are the stated purposes of pruning.
why.b: Wrong. Fruit quality is governed by variety and by harvesting time.
why.c: Wrong. None of these is given as a purpose.
why.d: Wrong. Pruning is not used to suppress flowering or fruiting.

prompt: The glossary defines pruning as the removal of dead or excess {{1}}, that is leaves.
explanation: Fronds. It is the proper word for palm leaves, and using it is what a wording question is testing.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the six common pests and diseases of oil palm?

options.text: Bagworms
Rhinoceros beetles
Saprolegnia
Ganoderma trunk rot

explanation: The six are bagworms, rhinoceros beetles, red spider mites, rodents, freckle disease and Ganoderma trunk rot. Saprolegnia is the fungus that infects fish skin and gills, from Module Two.

why.a: Wrong as an answer. Bagworms head the list of six.
why.b: Wrong as an answer. Rhinoceros beetles are second on the list.
why.c: Correct. Saprolegnia is a fish fungus, not an oil palm problem.
why.d: Wrong as an answer. Ganoderma trunk rot is the sixth item.

prompt: Among the oil palm diseases, {{1}} trunk rot is named alongside freckle disease.
explanation: Ganoderma. The three G names in this course are Ganoderma the palm fungus, Gyrodactylus the fish parasite, and Gallionella the iron bacterium.

prompt: Which set names oil palm pests rather than diseases?

options.text: Bagworms, rhinoceros beetles, red spider mites and rodents
Freckle disease and Ganoderma trunk rot
Aeromonas, Vibrio and Pseudomonas
Ichthyophthirius and Gyrodactylus

explanation: Four pests and two diseases make the six. The pests are bagworms, rhinoceros beetles, red spider mites and rodents; the diseases are freckle disease and Ganoderma trunk rot.

why.a: Correct. These four are the pests on the list.
why.b: Wrong. Those two are the diseases, not the pests.
why.c: Wrong. Those are harmful bacteria in fish ponds.
why.d: Wrong. Those are fish parasites.

prompt: How long after planting do oil palm trees begin producing harvestable fruit?

options.text: 3 to 4 years
12 to 15 months
70 to 80 days
6 to 8 years

explanation: 3 to 4 years after planting. It is also the reason intercropping is limited to the first 4 years: after that the palms take the light.

why.a: Correct. Harvestable fruit begins 3 to 4 years after planting.
why.b: Wrong. 12 to 15 months is the nursery period before planting.
why.c: Wrong. 70 to 80 days is the dormancy treatment.
why.d: Wrong. Well beyond the stated figure.

prompt: Oil palm begins producing harvestable fruit {{1}} years after planting.
explanation: 3 to 4 years. The intercropping window of 4 years is set by exactly this figure.

prompt: Which three signs show that fresh fruit bunches are ready for harvest?

options.text: Loose fruits falling to the ground, a change in fruit colour, and softening of the fruits
Fronds yellowing, trunk splitting, and roots surfacing
Flowering, pollination, and fruit set
Rising oil content measured in the laboratory

explanation: Loose fruits, colour change, softening. All three are visible from the ground, which is what makes them useful to a harvester.

why.a: Correct. These three are the ripeness signs.
why.b: Wrong. Those would be signs of disease or stress.
why.c: Wrong. Those come long before ripeness.
why.d: Wrong. No laboratory test is given as a harvest sign.

prompt: One sign that a fresh fruit bunch is ready for harvest is {{1}} fruits falling to the ground.
explanation: Loose fruits. Harvesting time matters because overripe or under-ripe fruit gives poor oil quality with high free fatty acids.

prompt: Which four tools are used for harvesting oil palm?

options.text: Chisel, harvesting hook, climbing rope, and mechanical harvester
Machete, hoe, rake, and wheelbarrow
Digester, press, clarifier, and fibre separator
Algae scraper, air stone, filter, and net

explanation: Chisel, hook, rope, mechanical harvester. The glossary splits the first two by tree height: the chisel for shorter trees, the hook for tall ones.

why.a: Correct. These four are the harvesting tools named.
why.b: Wrong. None of these appears as a harvesting tool in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Those are processing machines.
why.d: Wrong. Those are aquarium equipment from Module Two.

prompt: How does the glossary distinguish the harvesting hook from the chisel?

options.text: The hook is a curved tool for tall trees; the chisel is a flat-bladed tool for shorter trees
The hook is for shorter trees; the chisel is for tall trees
The hook cuts fronds; the chisel cuts fruit bunches
They are two names for the same tool

explanation: Hook for tall, chisel for short. The distinction is height, and it is the kind of small paired fact the examiner likes.

why.a: Correct. Curved hook for tall trees, flat-bladed chisel for shorter ones.
why.b: Wrong. This reverses the two.
why.c: Wrong. Both are for harvesting fruit bunches.
why.d: Wrong. The glossary defines them separately.

prompt: The {{1}} is a flat-bladed tool used for harvesting fruit bunches from shorter oil palm trees.
explanation: Chisel. The curved harvesting hook does the same job on tall trees.

prompt: Where is palm oil extracted from, and how widely is it used?

options.text: From the mesocarp, and it is one of the most widely used vegetable oils in the world
From the kernel, and it is used only in West Africa
From the empty fruit bunch, and it is used only as biofuel
From the fronds, and it is used only in cosmetics

explanation: Mesocarp, and one of the most widely used vegetable oils in the world. Its uses run across food, cosmetics and biofuel.

why.a: Correct. Palm oil comes from the mesocarp and is among the most widely used vegetable oils.
why.b: Wrong. The kernel gives palm kernel oil, and use is worldwide.
why.c: Wrong. Empty fruit bunches are a by-product, used as fertiliser and bioenergy.
why.d: Wrong. Fronds are pruned; they yield no oil.

prompt: Palm oil is one of the most widely used {{1}} oils in the world.
explanation: Vegetable. Module Three's closing summary calls oil palm processing a critical component of the global vegetable oil market.

prompt: Which set gives the food industry uses of palm oil?

options.text: Margarine and shortening, cooking oil, baked goods, confectionery and snack foods
Soaps, shampoos and moisturizers
Livestock feed and organic fertilizer
Biomass energy and animal bedding

explanation: Five food uses. The soaps and shampoos answer is the cosmetics list, the livestock feed answer is palm kernel cake, and the biomass energy answer is palm pressed fibre, so each wrong answer belongs to a different product.

why.a: Correct. These five are the food industry uses of palm oil.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the cosmetics and personal care uses.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the uses of palm kernel cake.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the uses of palm pressed fibre.

prompt: Palm oil is used as a feedstock for {{1}} production.
explanation: Biodiesel. Do not confuse it with biogas, which is what POME becomes in an anaerobic digester.

prompt: Which uses does the text give for palm kernel oil?

options.text: Frying and baking, margarine production, soap manufacturing, detergents, and cosmetic products
Livestock feed and organic fertilizer only
Biomass energy and animal bedding only
Compost and biodegradable building materials only

explanation: Five uses, and the deck shortens them to soap and baking. Note the overlap with palm oil: both make margarine and both reach cosmetics.

why.a: Correct. These five are the palm kernel oil uses.
why.b: Wrong. Those are palm kernel cake uses.
why.c: Wrong. Those are palm pressed fibre uses.
why.d: Wrong. Those are empty fruit bunch uses.

prompt: Palm kernel oil is extracted from the {{1}} or seed of the oil palm fruit.
explanation: Kernel. The pair to hold: mesocarp gives palm oil, kernel gives palm kernel oil.

prompt: Why is palm kernel oil more suitable than palm oil for high-temperature applications like frying?

options.text: It has a higher smoke point
It has a lower free fatty acid content by definition
It is extracted mechanically rather than chemically
It contains no saturated fat

explanation: A higher smoke point. It is the one technical difference the text draws between the two oils, and it appears in the in-text answer.

why.a: Correct. The in-text answer names the higher smoke point.
why.b: Wrong. Free fatty acid content depends on handling and processing, not on which oil it is.
why.c: Wrong. Palm kernel oil is extracted both mechanically and chemically.
why.d: Wrong. No such claim is made in the course.

prompt: Palm kernel oil suits frying because of its higher {{1}} point.
explanation: Smoke point. Both oils have similar uses; this is the property that separates them at high heat.

prompt: What is palm kernel cake, and what is it used for?

options.text: The residue left after oil extraction, used as livestock feed and organic fertilizer
The fibrous residue after oil extraction, used for biomass energy
The bunches left after fruit removal, used as compost
The wastewater from oil extraction, requiring treatment

explanation: The residue from the kernel, used as feed and fertilizer. The fibrous residue, the bunches left after fruit removal and the wastewater are palm pressed fibre, empty fruit bunches and POME, so all four by-products appear together here.

why.a: Correct. Palm kernel cake is the residue left after oil extraction, used as livestock feed and organic fertilizer.
why.b: Wrong. That is palm pressed fibre.
why.c: Wrong. Those are empty fruit bunches.
why.d: Wrong. That is palm oil mill effluent, POME.

prompt: Palm kernel cake is used as livestock feed and as organic {{1}}.
explanation: Organic fertilizer. The deck shortens it to animal feed, but the text gives both uses.

prompt: What is palm pressed fibre, and what two uses does it have?

options.text: The fibrous residue remaining after oil extraction, used for biomass energy production and animal bedding
The solid residue from the kernel, used as livestock feed
The wastewater from milling, used for irrigation
The shell of the nut, used as fuel for the boiler

explanation: Fibrous residue, biomass energy and animal bedding. The in-text answer calls the first use biofuels, processed into biomass for energy production.

why.a: Correct. Palm pressed fibre is the fibrous residue, used for biomass energy and animal bedding.
why.b: Wrong. That is palm kernel cake.
why.c: Wrong. POME is the wastewater, and it requires treatment before discharge.
why.d: Wrong. The shell is not given a use in this course.

prompt: Palm pressed fibre is used for biomass energy production and for animal {{1}}.
explanation: Bedding. Keep it apart from palm kernel cake, which is animal feed: fibre for bedding, cake for feed.

prompt: What are empty fruit bunches, and what three uses does the text give them?

options.text: The bunches left after the fruits are removed, used as organic fertilizer, for biomass energy, and for biodegradable building materials
The husks of the kernel, used only as boiler fuel
The fibre from the mesocarp, used as animal bedding
The sludge from clarification, used as compost only

explanation: Three uses, and the third is the distinctive one: biodegradable building materials. The processing unit adds composting as a sustainable practice for them.

why.a: Correct. Fertilizer, biomass energy and biodegradable building materials.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Kernel husks are not what EFB are.
why.c: Wrong. That is palm pressed fibre.
why.d: Wrong. Sludge is separated during clarification; EFB are the stripped bunches.

prompt: Empty fruit bunches can be used for organic fertilizer, biomass energy, and biodegradable {{1}} materials.
explanation: Building materials. It is the third use, the one candidates forget, because the first two are shared with other by-products.

prompt: Fruit types refer to which aspect of the oil palm fruit, and how many are there?

options.text: External morphology, and there are five
Internal genetics, and there are three
Oil content, and there are four
Harvest timing, and there are two

explanation: External morphology, five types. Species, by contrast, reflect internal genetic differences and there are three of them. Confusing the two classifications is the single easiest mark to lose in this unit.

why.a: Correct. Fruit types are external morphology: Nigrescens, Virescens, Albescens, Mantle or Poisson, and Parthenocarpic.
why.b: Wrong. Internal genetics with three members describes the species: Dura, Pisifera, Tenera.
why.c: Wrong. Oil content is a consequence, not the basis of the classification.
why.d: Wrong. Harvest timing is not a classification at all.

prompt: There are {{1}} oil palm fruit types, classified by external morphology.
explanation: Five fruit types against three species. Five and three is the pair to remember.

prompt: Which fruit type is black with an ivory colour towards the base when unripe, and turns red when ripe with the top half remaining black?

options.text: Nigrescens
Virescens
Albescens
Parthenocarpic

explanation: Nigrescens, the ordinary fruits. The name follows the colour: niger for black, and the black pigment is anthocyanin.

why.a: Correct. Black with ivory base when unripe, red when ripe with a black top half.
why.b: Wrong. Virescens is green when unripe.
why.c: Wrong. Albescens is white when unripe.
why.d: Wrong. Parthenocarpic fruits are defined by having no seeds.

prompt: {{1}} are the ordinary oil palm fruits, black when unripe and red when ripe with the top half staying black.
explanation: Nigrescens. The glossary connects it to anthocyanin, the pigment responsible for purple or black coloration.

prompt: Why are Virescens fruits green when unripe?

options.text: Because of a marked absence of the anthocyanin pigment
Because of a marked absence of carotenoid
Because they lack a mesocarp
Because they are harvested too early

explanation: No anthocyanin, so no black. When ripe they turn light reddish orange with greenish tips. Carotenoid is the pigment missing from Albescens, not Virescens.

why.a: Correct. Virescens lacks anthocyanin, the black and purple pigment.
why.b: Wrong. Absence of carotenoid is what makes Albescens white.
why.c: Wrong. All these fruit types have a mesocarp.
why.d: Wrong. The colour is genetic, not a matter of harvest timing.

prompt: Ripe Virescens fruits are light reddish orange with {{1}} tips.
explanation: Greenish tips. Each fruit type keeps a trace of its unripe colour when ripe, which is how the three colour types are told apart.

prompt: Albescens fruits are white when unripe. Why, and what colour do they become when ripe?

options.text: Because of the marked absence of carotenoid, and they turn pale yellow
Because of the marked absence of anthocyanin, and they turn red
Because they are parthenocarpic, and they stay white
Because they have no mesocarp, and they turn black

explanation: No carotenoid, so no orange or yellow while unripe; at ripeness they reach pale yellow. Anthocyanin is the pigment Virescens lacks.

why.a: Correct. Absence of carotenoid, turning pale yellow when ripe.
why.b: Wrong. Anthocyanin is what Virescens lacks.
why.c: Wrong. Parthenocarpic is a separate fruit type, defined by having no seeds.
why.d: Wrong. All these types have a mesocarp.

prompt: Albescens fruits are white when unripe due to the marked absence of {{1}}.
explanation: Carotenoid. The two pigment facts are the pair to drill: Virescens lacks anthocyanin, Albescens lacks carotenoid.

prompt: What are Mantle or Poisson fruits?

options.text: Fruits with a fleshy, oily outer growth developed from the carpel, which increases the mesocarp's overall oil content
Fruits with no seeds
Fruits with a very thick shell and no fibre ring
Fruits that never ripen

explanation: An extra fleshy, oily growth from the carpel, and it raises the oil content of the mesocarp. It is the only fruit type with a yield consequence attached.

why.a: Correct. This is the description of Mantle or Poisson fruits.
why.b: Wrong. Seedless fruits are Parthenocarpic.
why.c: Wrong. A thick shell with no fibre ring describes the Dura variety.
why.d: Wrong. No such type appears in the course.

prompt: What defines Parthenocarpic oil palm fruits?

options.text: They have no seeds, forming without fertilisation
They have two seeds each
They ripen before the rest of the bunch
They have the thickest shell of any type

explanation: No seeds. The glossary adds the mechanism: they form without fertilisation, which is what parthenocarpy means.

why.a: Correct. Parthenocarpic fruits are fruits with no seeds.
why.b: Wrong. The defining feature is the absence of seeds.
why.c: Wrong. Ripening order is not part of the classification.
why.d: Wrong. Shell thickness distinguishes the varieties Dura, Pisifera and Tenera.

prompt: {{1}} fruits are fruits with no seeds, which form without fertilisation.
explanation: Parthenocarpic. Do not confuse it with Pisifera, the shell-less variety whose problem is poor fertilisation and a high abortion ratio.

prompt: The species of oil palm fruits reflect which differences, and which three are they?

options.text: Internal, genetic differences: Dura, Pisifera and Tenera
External morphology: Nigrescens, Virescens and Albescens
Harvest timing: early, mid and late
Oil content: low, medium and high

explanation: Internal genetics, three species. This is the classification that decides shell thickness, fibre ring and commercial value.

why.a: Correct. Dura, Pisifera and Tenera reflect internal, genetic differences.
why.b: Wrong. Those are three of the five fruit types, which are external morphology.
why.c: Wrong. No timing classification exists in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Oil yield follows from the species; it is not the basis of the classification.

prompt: The species of oil palm fruits reflect the {{1}}, genetic differences of the palm fruits.
explanation: Internal. Fruit types are external morphology; species are internal genetics. One word separates the two classifications.

prompt: Which description matches Dura, coded DD?

options.text: Thick endocarp or shell, no fibre ring, the common wild palm type of natural habitats
Very thin or no shell, thick mesocarp, kernel surrounded by a fibre ring, poor fertilisation
Relatively thick mesocarp with a fibre ring, shells thinner than Dura, the recommended variety
Fruits with no seeds at all

explanation: Thick shell, no fibre ring, common in the wild. Its thick shell is why it yields less oil than Tenera.

why.a: Correct. Dura has a thick endocarp, no fibre ring, and is the common wild type.
why.b: Wrong. That is Pisifera.
why.c: Wrong. That is Tenera.
why.d: Wrong. That is the Parthenocarpic fruit type, not a species.

prompt: Dura is coded DD and has a thick endocarp, that is a thick {{1}}.
explanation: Shell. Endocarp and shell are the same thing here, and shell thickness is what the three species are sorted by.

prompt: What is the drawback of Pisifera, coded PF?

options.text: Fertilisation is poor, hence a high abortion ratio
Its shell is too thick to crack
It produces no mesocarp
It cannot survive tropical rainfall

explanation: Poor fertilisation and a high abortion ratio, which is why Pisifera is used as a breeding parent rather than planted commercially.

why.a: Correct. Poor fertilisation, hence a high abortion ratio.
why.b: Wrong. Pisifera has a very thin shell or none at all; Dura is the thick-shelled one.
why.c: Wrong. Pisifera has a thick mesocarp.
why.d: Wrong. No such limitation is described.

prompt: Pisifera has a very thin or no shell, but a thick mesocarp and a kernel surrounded by a {{1}} ring.
explanation: Fibre ring. Its presence or absence is the second distinguishing feature after shell thickness: Dura has none, Pisifera and Tenera have one.

prompt: Why is Tenera, coded DP, the recommended variety for cultivation?

options.text: It combines the characteristics of Dura and Pisifera, with a relatively thick mesocarp and a fibre ring, fruits larger than Pisifera and shells thinner than Dura
It has the thickest shell of the three, protecting the kernel
It is the common wild palm of natural habitats
It produces seedless fruit, which is easier to process

explanation: The best of both parents: thick oil-bearing mesocarp with a thin shell, so more of the fruit is oil and less of it is waste.

why.a: Correct. Thicker mesocarp, fibre ring, larger than Pisifera, thinner shell than Dura.
why.b: Wrong. A thick shell reduces oil yield, and that is Dura.
why.c: Wrong. The common wild type is Dura.
why.d: Wrong. Seedlessness describes Parthenocarpic fruits.

prompt: Tenera is coded {{1}}, reflecting its Dura and Pisifera parentage.
explanation: DP. The three codes are Dura DD, Pisifera PF and Tenera DP.

prompt: Which crops can be intercropped with newly established oil palm, and for how long?

options.text: Cassava, maize, sweet potatoes and melon, during the first 4 years
Rice, cocoa and rubber, during the first 10 years
Only maize, during the first year
Cassava and yam, for the whole life of the plantation

explanation: Four crops, four years. The window closes at 4 years because the palms start fruiting at 3 to 4 years and take the light.

why.a: Correct. Cassava, maize, sweet potatoes and melon in the first 4 years.
why.b: Wrong. None of those three is named, and 10 years is far beyond the window.
why.c: Wrong, and the word only cuts out three of the four crops.
why.d: Wrong. The window is the first 4 years, not the whole plantation life.

prompt: Intercropping with cassava, maize, sweet potatoes and melon runs during the first {{1}} years of the oil palm.
explanation: Four years. It matches the upper end of the 3 to 4 years to first harvest.

prompt: What must accompany intercropping, and why?

options.text: Good fertility management practices, to check fertility degradation, erosion and other problems
Complete removal of all weeds by herbicide only
Doubling the spacing between palms
Delaying the first fertiliser application by two years

explanation: Good fertility management. Two crops on one piece of land draw more from the soil, so degradation and erosion have to be watched.

why.a: Correct. Fertility management is required to check degradation and erosion.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Weeding is one agronomic practice among four.
why.c: Wrong. Spacing is fixed at 9 m by 9 m triangular.
why.d: Wrong. No such delay is recommended.

prompt: What benefits does the deck give for intercropping oil palm?

options.text: It improves income and supports better farm management
It removes the need for fertiliser
It shortens the time to first harvest
It raises the oil content of the fruit

explanation: Income and management. The text adds that care can be given simultaneously to two or more crops, which is what better management means here.

why.a: Correct. Improves income, supports better farm management.
why.b: Wrong. Fertility management becomes more important, not less.
why.c: Wrong. First harvest is 3 to 4 years regardless.
why.d: Wrong. Oil content depends on the variety and on harvest timing.

prompt: Which step of nursery management does the self-assessment answer place immediately before transplanting?

options.text: Hardening off
Seed germination
Seed selection and treatment
Weed and pest control

explanation: Hardening off. The six steps run: seed selection and treatment, germination, watering and fertilisation, weed and pest control, hardening off, transplanting.

why.a: Correct. Hardening off comes last before transplanting.
why.b: Wrong. Germination is the second step.
why.c: Wrong. Selection and treatment is the first step.
why.d: Wrong. Weed and pest control is the fourth step.

prompt: The self-assessment answer gives {{1}} steps of nursery management, from seed selection to transplanting.
explanation: Six steps. They sit inside the second of the five cultivation stages, nursery management.

prompt: In the self-assessment answer, at what age and height are seedlings ready for field planting?

options.text: After 12 to 18 months, when they reach 30 to 40 cm in height
After 12 to 15 months, when they reach 60 to 80 cm
After 3 to 4 years, at any height
After 70 to 80 days, when the first leaf opens

explanation: 12 to 18 months and 30 to 40 cm, as the self-assessment answer gives it. Note that the unit body says 12 to 15 months, so the course text is not internally consistent here; both figures come from the same book and either may be quoted.

why.a: Correct. This is the self-assessment answer word for word.
why.b: Wrong. 12 to 15 months is the unit body's figure, but the height given is not 60 to 80 cm.
why.c: Wrong. 3 to 4 years is the time to first harvest after planting.
why.d: Wrong. 70 to 80 days at 40 degrees Celsius is the dormancy treatment.

prompt: In the self-assessment answer, seedlings are ready for field planting when they reach {{1}} cm in height.
explanation: 30 to 40 cm. Height and age are given together: 12 to 18 months and 30 to 40 cm.

prompt: What is hardening off?

options.text: Gradually exposing seedlings to more sunlight and less frequent watering a few weeks before transplanting, to toughen them
Compacting the soil in the polybag before planting
Drying the seeds before cracking
Allowing the shell to thicken before harvest

explanation: More sun, less water, a few weeks before transplanting. It prepares the seedling for field conditions, which is the plant equivalent of acclimatising new fish.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition given in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong. No soil compaction step appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Nut drying before cracking belongs to palm kernel processing.
why.d: Wrong. Shell thickness is genetic, set by the variety.

prompt: How does the glossary define the mesocarp?

options.text: The fleshy middle layer of the oil palm fruit, from which palm oil is extracted
The hard shell surrounding the kernel
The stalk that holds the bunch together
The fibre left after pressing

explanation: The fleshy middle layer, source of palm oil. Digesting exists precisely to separate it from the kernel.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry.
why.b: Wrong. The shell is the endocarp.
why.c: Wrong. The stalk is what threshing removes the fruits from.
why.d: Wrong. That is palm pressed fibre.

prompt: Propagation is the process of {{1}} oil palm plants, commonly through seeds or tissue culture.
explanation: Reproducing. It is the first of the five cultivation stages.

prompt: Field establishment covers which activities, according to the glossary?

options.text: Preparing land for planting, including clearing, spacing and pegging
Growing seedlings in polythene bags
Weeding, fertilising, pruning and pest control
Cutting bunches with a chisel or hook

explanation: Clearing, spacing, pegging. It is the third of the five cultivation stages, between the nursery and the routine agronomic practices.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry for field establishment.
why.b: Wrong. That is nursery management.
why.c: Wrong. Those are agronomic practices.
why.d: Wrong. That is harvesting.

prompt: Anthocyanin is responsible for which coloration in oil palm fruit?

options.text: The purple or black colour of types like Nigrescens
The white colour of Albescens
The green colour of Virescens
The orange colour of ripe palm oil

explanation: Purple or black, as in Nigrescens. Virescens is green precisely because it lacks anthocyanin.

why.a: Correct. Anthocyanin gives the purple and black coloration of Nigrescens.
why.b: Wrong. Albescens is white because carotenoid is absent.
why.c: Wrong. Virescens is green because anthocyanin is absent.
why.d: Wrong. Carotenoid pigments account for the orange of palm oil, and the glossary does not attribute it to anthocyanin.

prompt: {{1}} is the pigment responsible for the purple or black coloration in oil palm fruit types like Nigrescens.
explanation: Anthocyanin. Two pigments, two absences: Virescens has no anthocyanin, Albescens has no carotenoid.

prompt: Mulching is covering the soil surface with materials like dry leaves to conserve moisture, suppress weeds and reduce {{1}}.
explanation: Erosion. Three benefits: moisture, weeds, erosion. The unit body names the first two, and the glossary adds the third.

prompt: How does the glossary define intercropping?

options.text: Growing other crops like maize or cassava alongside young oil palm trees to maximise land use and maintain fertility
Planting two varieties of oil palm in alternate rows
Rotating oil palm with a different crop every four years
Grafting one crop onto the rootstock of another

explanation: Other crops alongside young palms, for land use and fertility. Young is the operative word: the practice stops after 4 years.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry for intercropping.
why.b: Wrong. Mixing varieties is not what intercropping means.
why.c: Wrong. That would be crop rotation, and oil palm is a perennial.
why.d: Wrong. No grafting appears in the course.

prompt: Which statement matches the deck's closing summary of oil palm cultivation?

options.text: Oil palm is a major tropical oil crop, requires proper nursery and field management, and timely harvesting improves yield
Oil palm is a temperate crop that fruits within its first year
Oil palm produces no by-products of industrial value
Oil palm should be grown without any agronomic intervention

explanation: Tropical, well managed, timely harvest, valuable by-products. Every clause is a summary of a section of the unit.

why.a: Correct. This is the deck's conclusion.
why.b: Wrong. It is tropical and fruits at 3 to 4 years.
why.c: Wrong. The by-products are the subject of a whole section.
why.d: Wrong. Four routine agronomic practices are prescribed.

prompt: On what does successful oil palm cultivation depend, according to the unit conclusion?

options.text: Proper nursery management, field establishment, agronomic practices, and timely harvesting
Sterilisation, threshing, digesting and pressing
Market demand, cost of inputs, profit margin and scalability
Planning, organising, controlling and directing

explanation: Four of the five cultivation stages, with propagation assumed. Understanding them is called essential for maximising yield, sustainability and profitability.

why.a: Correct. These four are named in the conclusion.
why.b: Wrong. Those are processing stages from Unit 2.
why.c: Wrong. Those are agribusiness evaluation criteria from Module Four.
why.d: Wrong. That is POCD, from Module Four Unit 3.

prompt: Match each oil palm name to what it describes.

pairs.right: Thick shell, no fibre ring, common wild type
Thin or no shell, poor fertilisation
The recommended hybrid, thin shell and thick mesocarp
Black when unripe, red when ripe
White when unripe, pale yellow when ripe

explanation: Three varieties and two fruit types side by side. Varieties are internal genetics; fruit types are external colour.

prompt: Match each oil palm figure to what it measures.

pairs.right: Palms per hectare at 9 m by 9 m triangular

explanation: The five headline figures of the cultivation unit. The spare labels belong to 70 to 80 days, 12 to 15 months and 56 g, which are the other three numbers to hold.

prompt: The five stages of oil palm cultivation are {{1}}, and the crop first fruits {{2}}.

accept: propagation, nursery management, field establishment, agronomic practices and harvesting
choices: propagation, nursery management, field establishment, agronomic practices and harvesting
sterilisation, threshing, digesting, pressing and clarification
fibre separation, nut drying, cracking, extraction and storage
planning, organising, directing, controlling and reviewing
in the first rainy season after planting

explanation: The sequence and the timeline together. Every other date in the unit hangs off these: 12 to 15 months in the nursery before planting, 4 years of intercropping after it, and first fruit at 3 to 4 years.

prompt: The four oil palm harvesting tools are the chisel, the harvesting hook, the climbing rope and the mechanical {{1}}.
explanation: Mechanical harvester. Do not reach for digester, thresher or fibre separator: those are processing machines, not harvesting tools.

prompt: The mesocarp is the fleshy {{1}} layer of the oil palm fruit, from which palm oil is extracted.
explanation: Middle layer. The unit body calls it the fleshy outer part of the fruit and the glossary calls it the middle layer; both point at the same tissue, the one that yields palm oil.
